title: Oil Rebounds Through Hormuz While LNG Stays Blocked as Qatar Extends Force Majeure; Trump Signs Venezuela Reserves Deal
subhead: Ship-tracking data shows Gulf oil flows recovering to roughly two-thirds of prewar levels via tanker shuttling and sales outside the strait, even as LNG traffic remains at a standstill and Qatar extends force majeure into November. President Trump formally announced an agreement giving US companies majority control of 65+ billion barrels of Venezuela's proven reserves.

sections.heading: Hormuz Oil Flows Rebound Even as Tanker Traffic Stays Subdued
sections.body:
The Iran war is entering its seventh month with a striking divergence at the Strait of Hormuz: oil volumes are flowing again, but actual vessel traffic is not. Goldman Sachs estimates oil flows out of the strait have recovered to about two-thirds of prewar levels, according to Bloomberg, while unnamed traders quoted by Bloomberg put the current rate at 6 to 8 million barrels per day.

That recovery is not reflected in ship counts. Reuters, citing preliminary Kpler data, reported just 7 commodity vessels transiting Hormuz on Thursday, down from 17 a day earlier and below the 10-day average of 15 — versus roughly 130 ships a day before the war. Maritime data firm Windward counted six tankers passing on Thursday, three of them running in 'dark mode' to avoid detection. The gap is explained by how producers adapt: ING analysts note more Gulf producers are shuttling crude through the strait and selling oil outside Hormuz entirely, using ship-to-ship transfers and alternate routes that keep volumes moving without a return to normal convoy traffic.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first sustained evidence that oil markets can partially reroute around the chokepoint — explaining why Brent has slid rather than spiked. But the recovery depends on costly shuttling and stealth, not a normal reopening, so the constraint on Gulf exports is easing slowly, not ending.

sections.heading: LNG Stays Fully Blocked as Qatar Extends Force Majeure Through November
sections.body:
Unlike crude, liquefied natural gas cannot be shuttle-shipped through Hormuz and reloaded, and Friday brought confirmation the impasse will persist: reports cited by Oilprice.com and Bloomberg said QatarEnergy has extended its force majeure on LNG deliveries into October-early November. LNG traffic through the strait remains at a standstill even as oil flows rise.

The knock-on effect hit prices. Asian spot LNG jumped to $23.39 per million BTU on Friday, hovering at four-year highs, with Asian utilities outbidding Europe for a shrinking pool of cargoes. European benchmark TTF gas rose 2% to top $80 per megawatt-hour (about €69), its highest since 2023. Europe heads into winter with storage sites barely 63% full, per Oilprice.com, versus a five-year average near 80% — the result of summer heatwave demand and the collapse of Qatari term cargoes since the war began in February.
sections.whyItMatters: The oil-gas split is the real story of the war's seventh month: the market can improvise around Hormuz for oil, but the gas trade has no such workaround. That leaves Europe and Asia competing for scarce LNG just as winter approaches, with Qatar's cargoes trapped behind the strait.

sections.heading: Trump Formally Announced Venezuela Deal for Control of 65 Billion Barrels
sections.body:
President Donald Trump on Friday announced an unprecedented agreement granting US companies majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela's proven oil reserves — about a fifth of the country's total — through a partnership with private business, per USA Today. In a Truth Social post, Trump said Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, working with interim President Delcy Rodriguez, had 'secured majority U.S. control' of the reserves 'at no cost to the American Taxpayer.'

Rodriguez, who took over after the US seized Nicolas Maduro in January, welcomed the deal, saying development of 17 strategic fields would boost production and deliver $209 billion in tax revenue. Rubio called it a win-win, citing roughly $100 billion in private investment. Yet the details remain thin — Trump did not disclose the legal structure, fields or companies involved. Reuters has reported a lease model is under consideration, with fields potentially auctioned to US producers, and that the arrangement could face constitutional and legal challenges given Venezuela's state control over core oil activities. Separate reporting has raised the possibility Venezuela could pull out of OPEC as part of the realignment.
sections.whyItMatters: The deal converts an intervention into a permanent supply fixture for US refineries at a moment the strategic reserve is at a 40-year low. But the missing legal framework, the state-control question and the taxpayer cost Trump denies are all unresolved, meaning the headline number is bigger than the reality so far.

sections.heading: Bessent Says Pipelines Will Make Hormuz 'Irrelevant' — Experts Say Not Soon
sections.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued the strait 'is going to become irrelevant' within two years, telling an NBC affiliate that 50% to 70% of energy products normally shipped through Hormuz would move via underground pipelines. In an NPR fact-check Friday, energy analysts and the IEA pushed back sharply.

The IEA's senior oil market analyst Rebecca Schulz told NPR that even after planned projects finish, the oil still needing to pass through Hormuz for total Gulf exports to return to prewar levels could exceed 10 million barrels per day — around half of prewar flows. The UAE expects a $3 billion expansion to its Fujairah export port to come online next year, but a larger Saudi pipeline expansion will take several more years, per the IEA. Oil major TotalEnergies said this week it is profitably moving steeply discounted oil through Hormuz and will invest in expanding its Fujairah pipeline in Abu Dhabi. Former US State Department special envoy David Goldwyn told NPR the export constraints are likely a 'somewhat permanent' feature for the next few years.
sections.whyItMatters: The debate over whether pipelines can replace Hormuz is central to how markets price the war's duration. Bessent's timeline assumes infrastructure that doesn't exist yet; the IEA and company plans suggest a partial, multi-year shift at best — leaving a persistent premium on Gulf crude.

sections.heading: Japan Moves to Diversify Crude Away From Hormuz as Six-Month Mark Passes
sections.body:
Japan, which sourced almost all of its imported crude through the Strait of Hormuz before the war, unveiled a plan to strengthen energy-supply resilience, including backing pipeline projects that bypass the strait, Reuters reported, citing media sources. The move directly reflects the war's toll on a country with no domestic production and heavy reliance on Gulf oil.

The announcement lands as the conflict marks its six-month anniversary. Reuters' commentary describes the war 'sinking into energy trench warfare,' a stalemate that could last into 2027 with energy markets held hostage. President Trump insists Iran is 'begging to make a deal,' while Tehran and Beijing say his economic pressure campaign has not worked, per CBS News and Yahoo. Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said Friday that 'putting diplomacy back on track isn't impossible' but warned against preconditions, even as CENTCOM said it has cleared the strait of Iranian sea mines and Iran offered only a temporary, limited transit corridor.
sections.whyItMatters: Japan's diversification is a concrete, sovereign response to the war that, alongside Emirati and Saudi pipeline work and China's reduced import appetite, signals that the Hormuz shock is prompting lasting supply-chain redesign rather than a quick return to prewar routing.

sections.heading: Iran Touts New Gas Discovery and Russian Energy Ties Even as Sanctions Bite
sections.body:
Even as the US widens sanctions aimed at cutting off Iran's economic lifeline, Tehran announced a discovery of 7.5 trillion cubic feet (21.24 billion cubic meters) of natural gas in Fars province, Iran's oil minister Mohsen Paknejad said, with the recoverable portion roughly equal to 15 years of output from the first phase of the giant South Pars field, per WION, TeleSUR and Bloomberg. The announcement underscored the squeeze the war has put on Iranian energy production and monetization.

Iran has also been touting a Russian energy deal, part of a broader effort to line up buyers and partners outside the US-led financial system, per regional wire coverage. The parallel tracks — a propaganda-ready resource announcement and deepening Russian ties — come as Washington's 'Operation Economic Outcast' campaign designates third-country intermediaries, with China as Iran's main buyer of discounted crude, leaving Beijing in a dilemma over how far to defy US dollar-based pressure.
sections.whyItMatters: Iran signaling new gas resources and closer Russian energy cooperation is largely symbolic given it cannot export much under blockade and sanctions. But it frames Tehran's endgame: resist long enough for its own reserves to retain value and for Washington's coalition to fracture, rather than accept a bad deal now.

bottomLine: The defining development of the seventh month of the Iran war is a split screen at Hormuz: Gulf oil flows have partially recovered to roughly two-thirds of prewar levels through tanker shuttling and sales outside the strait — enough to keep prices from spiking — while LNG remains fully blocked and Qatar extends force majeure into November, pushing European storage toward winter at barely 63% full and spot gas to multi-year highs. Washington offered its own supply-side answer on Friday, formally announcing a deal for US majority control of 65+ billion barrels of Venezuela's reserves, though legal and cost questions remain unresolved. The through-line: markets are learning to adapt around the chokepoint for oil but not for gas, and both the US (Venezuela deals, pipeline claims) and its adversaries (Japan's diversification, Iran's Russian pivot) are locking in longer-term supply redesigns that assume the Hormuz constraint will not vanish quickly.
sources: USA Today, Reuters, Bloomberg, Oilprice.com, NPR, Kpler, Windward, ING, IEA, Goldman Sachs, CBS News, Yahoo News, WION, TeleSUR, Washington Post, Newsweek, Cyprus Mail
